title: Where did it begin
hook: the yogis ask about the very beginning, and Nanak answers with wonder

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis offered their earrings, and Nanak named the Word as the earring worn within. Your line was the word as earring. Did it catch the light? Today the questions get bigger. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

What was there before there was anything? Small children ask it at bedtime, usually right after the light goes off. Physicists ask it with chalk. And in the Sidh Gosht, the yogis ask it of Nanak. So far they've asked about him: who he is, how he lives, why he travels, what he wears. Now they ask about everything. What can you say about the beginning? Before anything was made, where was the void, the sunn, at home? Today: where did it begin, and an answer that starts with a single word.
screen: `BEFORE THERE WAS ANYTHING?` → `THE YOGIS ASK ABOUT EVERYTHING.` → `WHERE WAS THE VOID AT HOME?`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of Nanak's answer, in paraphrase. Of the beginning, all one can speak of is wonder. The One dwelt then in itself, in the void, without end. The word for wonder is bismaad. It's the word Sikhs use for awe so large it leaves you without anything to add. Notice what Nanak doesn't do. He doesn't hand the yogis a list of steps, first this, then that. He doesn't give a date or a mechanism. Asked the biggest question there is, he gives a one-word answer: wonder. That's not a refusal. It's a report. In this poem, the beginning is the kind of thing that is met with astonishment, not with a diagram. Then he takes the yogis' own word, sunn, the void, and doesn't argue with it. The word belonged to their own practice. Nanak agrees there was a void before all things. He just says who was there: the One, dwelling in itself. The emptiness wasn't empty. In the Japji, near its start, there's a similar move: the One before the ages, true in the beginning. And elsewhere the Guru Granth Sahib speaks of a long darkness before creation, where only the divine order was. The texts don't try to make the beginning ordinary. They let it stay huge. That's worth carrying out the door. The coffee, the birdsong, the fact that there's anything at all instead of nothing: in this poem, the right first response to all of it is bismaad. That's the line. It began in wonder.
screen: `OF THE BEGINNING: ONLY WONDER.` · `BISMAAD, AWE WITHOUT WORDS.` · `NO STEPS, NO DATE, NO MECHANISM.` · `THE VOID WASN'T EMPTY.` · then, large: `IT BEGAN IN WONDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in wonder. Let the breath slow. Then choose one ordinary thing within reach of your senses: your own hand, the light in the room, a sound outside. Look at it, or listen, as if it had only just appeared. Then let the question come gently: why is this here at all, instead of nothing? Don't try to answer. Nanak didn't give the yogis a mechanism, and you don't need one either. Just let the astonishment be there, even a small amount. When the mind starts explaining, come back to looking. If you pray, you can let that astonishment be the prayer, without words. The bell holds the time.
Where did it begin. The yogis' question about the beginning, and Nanak's answer: of that, one can only speak with wonder, and the One dwelt in the void. Today's word.
Your line: it began in wonder. Once today, stop in front of something ordinary, a tree, a cup, a face, and let it astonish you for one breath. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 1137 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DOES THE MIND LIVE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of bismaad, wonder or awe, as a fitting response to the Creator and creation, and the Sidh Gosht's answer about the beginning is read in katha alongside the Japji's opening and the hymns of the time before creation.

original.note: bismaad: wonder, awe; Nanak's one-word answer about the beginning.

trapdoor: what you thought: the yogis wanted a creation story with steps.
what it means: Nanak says of the beginning one can only speak of wonder, and the One dwelt in the void.
what a scholar hears: Nanak keeps the yogis' own term, sunn, and fills it: the void of their meditation was the One, dwelling in itself.

notes: Sidh Gosht question and answer paraphrased (aad kau kavan beechaar katheealay, sunn kahaa ghar vaaso; aad kau bismaad beechaar katheealay, sunn nirantar vaas leeaa). Please confirm the pauri numbers (22–23) and Ang 940.
'Bismaad... the word Sikhs use for awe so large it leaves you without anything to add' is a gloss; please confirm it is fair.
The script says the yogis' meditation 'aimed at that emptiness'; a general description of the Nath goal of sunn samadhi. Please confirm wording.

Editor pass: cut 'on the third day the mountains' (read as a jab at another tradition's creation account, and inaccurate to it); cut 'the honest' and 'when you think about it properly, leaves you astonished' (told the listener what they feel); replaced 'their meditation aimed at that emptiness' with 'the word belonged to their own practice' (unsourced claim about Nath goals; the note above on that wording no longer applies); cut the etymology-style 'the word itself carries wonder' from the practice.
